title: Comparing durations
keyIdea: A duration is how long something takes. To compare two durations, start them at the same time: the one still going when the other stops takes longer, and the other takes a shorter time. We can measure time by counting steady claps. The same number of claps means the same time. In a race, the one who takes fewer claps is quicker and the one who takes more is slower. Ending last does not mean taking longest if it started late.

kid: Some things take a long time, like a night of sleep. Some take a short time, like a sneeze.
Start two things at the same time. Which one is still going when the other stops? That one takes longer.
We can count claps to measure time. Clap at the same speed. 6 claps and 6 claps is the same time. Fewer claps is quicker. More claps is slower.
Be careful. The one that ends last may have started late. Line up the starts, then look.
adult: England's Year 1 maths programme asks children to 'compare, describe and solve practical problems for time [for example, quicker, slower, earlier, later]' and to 'measure and begin to record time (hours, minutes, seconds)'. In the Early Years this starts as talk: which takes longer, which is shorter, the same time. Duration means how long an event lasts, from its start to its end.

Young children judge time the way they judge length: they compare by eye and by the end point. Just as two sticks must start at the same line to compare lengths, two events must start together, or be measured in the same units, before one can be called longer. Non-standard units such as claps, a sand timer or counting to ten come before seconds and minutes, and they only work if the beat stays steady.

Common mistakes: children often decide that the event which finishes last took the longest, even when it started later. In a race, many think more claps means quicker, but more claps means more time, so slower. Some mix up a long time with something big or far away. Others say two events are different when they take the same number of claps.

In the lab your child presses Play, so both bars grow together, and taps the one still going. Next they stretch a bar until two jobs take the same time. Then they slide a late snack back to the start line. Last, they pick the quicker runner by fewer claps and order three jobs from shortest to longest time.

familyTip: Race small jobs against each other: who can put their shoes on before the song ends? Clap or count together while two things happen, then ask which took longer. Use the words quicker, slower, longer and shorter time, and a sand timer or a kitchen timer to check.

visual.caption: Does it take a short time or a long time? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: start two jobs together, make two jobs take the same time, line up a late start, pick the quicker runner and order three jobs by time.

practice.prompt: Which takes longer: eating your lunch or blinking your eyes?
practice.hint: Think about starting both at the same time. Which one is still going?
practice.explain: A blink is over in a moment. Eating lunch keeps going for a long time, so it takes longer.

practice.prompt: A song takes {a} claps. Tidy up takes {b} claps. How many more claps does the song take?
practice.hint: Start from the bigger number of claps and count back the smaller number.
practice.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b}, so the song takes {=a-b} more claps. More claps means a longer time.

practice.prompt: Mia runs in {a} claps. Sam takes 2 more claps than Mia. How many claps does Sam take?
practice.hint: Start at Mia's claps and count on 2 more.
practice.explain: {a} + 2 = {=a+2}. Sam takes more claps, so Sam is slower and Mia is quicker.

practice.prompt: Ben tidies up in 4 claps. Ava tidies up in 7 claps. Who is quicker?
practice.explain: Ben takes 4 claps, fewer than 7, so Ben is quicker. Ava takes more time, so she is slower.

pool.hint: Which one is over almost as soon as it starts?
pool.explain: A sneeze is over in a moment. A night of sleep and a school day both go on for hours.

pool.prompt: A song takes 6 claps. A dance takes 6 claps. Which is true?
pool.hint: Compare the number of claps for each one.
pool.explain: 6 claps and 6 claps is the same number, so the song and the dance take the same time.

pool.prompt: The bath starts first. The snack starts later and ends last. How can you tell which takes longer?
choices: count the claps for each one
the one that ends last takes longer
the one that starts first takes longer
pool.hint: The end alone does not tell you. What do you need to know about the start too?
pool.explain: The snack may end last only because it started late. Count the claps from each start, or line up the starts, then compare.

pool.prompt: Two children race. Who is slower?
choices: the one who takes more claps
the one who takes fewer claps
pool.explain: Taking more claps means taking more time, so that child is slower. Being tall does not tell you the time.

pool.prompt: The sand timer runs out before the song ends. Which takes longer?
pool.hint: They started together. Which one is still going?
pool.explain: The song is still playing when the sand has run out, so the song takes longer.

pool.prompt: Putting on shoes takes {a} claps. Putting on a coat takes {b} claps. How many claps for both, one after the other?
pool.hint: Add the claps for the shoes and the claps for the coat.
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b}, so both jobs together take {=a+b} claps.

pool.prompt: A hop race takes {a} claps. A walk takes {b} claps more. How many claps does the walk take?
pool.hint: Start at the hop race claps and count on.
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b}. The walk takes more claps, so it takes a longer time.

pool.prompt: Put these in order from the shortest time to the longest: lunch, sneeze, putting on shoes.
pool.hint: Find the quickest one first, then the next, then the longest.
pool.explain: A sneeze is the shortest, putting on shoes takes a little while, and lunch takes the longest.
